@@CASE@@: Fig.~\ref{fig:case} shows two patterns on D4 at the threshold of $K=300$ ($\gamma=0.0017$) with the same point score, 0.0041. Blue points have positive and orange points negative posterior means, and fainter points have larger variances. The kept pattern \{Chinese restaurant, food and drink shop, salon/barbershop\} rests on 18 venues with a median of 5.5 training check-ins, and its lower bound is 0.0035. The rejected pattern \{bar, salon/barbershop\} rests on 329 venues with a median of two training check-ins, whose posterior variances add up to 184. Its lower bound is therefore 0.0010 with independent variances, already below $\gamma$, and falls to 0.0005 once the error of the estimated prior and center, shared by these venues, raises the variance to 245 (Definition~\ref{def:totalvar}). The variance of the kept pattern stays near 8.
@@EFFTEXT@@: Fig.~\ref{fig:eff} shows the mining time on D4 and D5, and Table~\ref{tab:ablation} the ablation. With $k=20$ features the pattern space is small (3,481 nodes on D4), and a bound evaluation costs about as much as the nodes it saves. At $K=300$, UHUCPM evaluates 38\% of the nodes of NoPrune on D4 in the same time, and at $K=1000$ it is slower than NoPrune on D4 and no faster on D5. The space grows exponentially with $k$ while the patterns above the threshold do not, so the bounds pay off as $k$ grows. At $k=80$ and $K=100$, UHUCPM evaluates 4.0\% and 0.56\% of the nodes of NoPrune on D4 and D5 and takes 1.9\,s against 18\,s and 53\,s against 1,274\,s. A lower threshold has the opposite effect, because it enlarges the part of the space that no bound can prune (Fig.~\ref{fig:eff}(a), (b)). The suffix bound matters most. Without it, UHUCPM evaluates 1.34 and 1.82 times as many nodes on D4 and D5, and a linear scan of the suffix bounds instead of the binary search takes 30\% and 12\% more time. At $z=1.645$ the exact bound evaluates about 9\% fewer nodes than the mean bound at a similar time, because the variance penalty is still small. It pays off at larger $z$. At $z=3.09$ ($\delta=0.001$) and $k=60$, it evaluates 18\% and 19\% fewer nodes on D4 and D5 and takes 11\% and 12\% less time. On EviGen with $k=10$, from $n=10^3$ to $10^5$, building the cliques grows as $n^{1.17}$ and mining as $n^{0.57}$. On the PSO-MUCP data, a whole run of UHUCPM, from process start to exit, takes 5.3--6.9\,s against 104--110\,s for the authors' code on California and 2.8--3.2\,s against 50--54\,s on Las Vegas (means of five runs), and both return the same result sets.
@@CALIBTOPIC@@: On semi-synthetic counts, UHUCPM keeps the FDP below $\delta$ and detects several to tens of times more true patterns than the other safe method, the shortcut.
@@PLBTEXT@@: The shortcut has an FDP of at most 0.003 but detects at most 2\% of the true patterns, against 11\%--12\% for UHUCPM on New York, and on Tokyo it reports nothing in most runs.
@@EVTEXT@@: The filter on median evidence, tuned to the output size of UHUCPM, reports 15\%--21\% false patterns on New York and 14\%--26\% on Tokyo, so thin evidence alone does not identify the false patterns.
@@VTONLY@@: a further 0\%--5\% of the patterns found with point utilities on D4 and D5. At $K=1000$ these few patterns, compared without pairing, hold in 2 of 11 and 9 of 13 cases, against 68\% and 85\% of the patterns kept with $V_T$.
@@EVREAL@@: A filter on the median evidence per instance comes closer, with a difference of 0.04 [$-$0.12, 0.23], but on semi-synthetic counts it reports 14\%--26\% false patterns (Table~\ref{tab:semisyn}).
@@EVLIMIT@@: On real data a filter on the median evidence holds about as often as UHUCPM, but it does not control the FDP when the truth is known.
